claims.statement: A JavaScript expression input is parsed as a single expression, not a script: a bare statement such as `var x = 1;` is a syntax error, and multi-statement logic must be wrapped in an IIFE — `(() => { ...; return value; })()` — which is itself an expression.
claims.rationale: Three benchmarked sessions hit `Unexpected token 'var'` and concluded multi-line JavaScript was impossible. The published `MaxStatements` sandbox option actively implies the opposite, and nothing published the rule.

claims.statement: The `RunJavaScript` activity's script input is the opposite case: the evaluator supplies the function body, so statements and a bare `return` work directly and must not be wrapped in an IIFE.
claims.rationale: The same source string is legal in one slot and a syntax error in the other; without this pair a consumer generalises the wrong half of the rule.

claims.statement: Required-output enforcement is per node and all-or-nothing: a node that authors no output bindings is never checked, and binding a single output makes every required output on that node mandatory — so `isRequired` means "must be bound if you bind anything here", not "the runtime fills this in".
claims.rationale: `HttpEndpoint` rejects a missing `RouteData` once `Request` is bound while `WriteHttpResponse` publishes with all four required outputs unbound; that looks like a per-activity difference and is one rule about binding state. `[Output]` defaults `IsRequired` to true, so most published `isRequired: true` values are an unreviewed default — pre-binding an output "to be safe" is what turns a working definition into a publish-time 400.

claims.statement: An HTTP `(route template, method)` pair is exclusive across workflow definitions — a second definition claiming a pair another definition already holds fails the publish — while republishing a definition into the slot it already occupies is exempt, and two definitions may hold the same template under different methods.
claims.rationale: The exclusivity is what makes a second run of the same authoring script fail where the first succeeded: submitting again creates a NEW definition, and that new definition then collides with the route the first one already claimed.

claims.statement: Submitting a definition whose name already exists creates a second, independent definition — a name is not an identity, and there is no upsert-by-name — so to add a version to an existing definition you must address that definition by id rather than re-submit its name.
claims.rationale: This is what makes route exclusivity bite on re-runs: running the same authoring script twice produces two definitions, and the second collides with the HTTP route the first already claimed.

claims.statement: An executable artifact id is derived from a hash of execution material only, so two definitions with identical authored behaviour share one artifact id regardless of which definition version, artifact version or source produced them — while any change to execution material (down to an input-binding literal) moves it.
claims.rationale: A consumer that assumes one artifact id per definition will read another definition's executions as its own; a consumer that assumes the id changes per publish will miss that a no-op republish reuses it.

claims.statement: A captured value's `preview` is capped at 256 characters by default and the capture then carries `truncated: true` alongside the value's real `length` — so an equality assertion against a captured value is only sound after checking `truncated` is false.
claims.rationale: A benchmarked session asserted equality against a 256-character prefix and read the mismatch as a workflow defect. The cap is a display bound, not a statement about what the workflow produced.

claims.statement: A captured JSON value (an `HttpEndpoint`'s `ParsedContent`, for instance) reaches a JavaScript expression under the `args` namespace as a native value — objects, arrays, numbers and booleans walkable with plain `args.name.field[0]` access, no accessor call and no `JSON.parse` — but every such object is frozen, so writing to one throws under the evaluator's strict-mode wrapper instead of being silently dropped.
claims.rationale: A benchmarked session published a throwaway probe workflow purely to learn this shape. The freezing matters separately: code that mutates its input as a scratch buffer fails at runtime rather than degrading quietly.
